newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says major changes needed to keep skies safe.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says major changes needed to keep skies safe.

text.p: Federal Aviation Administrator David Hinson warned on Wednesday that the number of airline crashes could increase if major strides were not taken to keep the skies safe.

He said at the National Press Club that between 1960 and 1995 the number of flights had doubled and passengers carried had tripled but the accident rate dropped by half. In the next 15 years, he said, U.S. airlines will be carrying more than a billion passengers, double today's number.

Hinson said the challenge was "to make sure we get that increment of improvement that we got between 1960 and 1995 so that when 20 years from now occurs we will be looking at an accident rate that is essentially zero."
To reach that goal, he said, "We are going to have to do some things differently because what got us to where we are today will not get us to where we have to go in 20 years. It will not."
Absent progress, he said, it is estimated there would be one major crash evry week or 10 days somewhere in the world.

But he said the surge in air travel will coincide with the shift from ground-based to space-based air traffic control, enabling controllers to handle the growth in air traffic with greater safety as well as greater efficiency.

Hinson said governments worldwide were recognising the need for uniform higher safety standards. He said the FAA was promoting a new programme to enable countries and airlines to exchange safety-related information they now routinely gather but also routinely discard.

Officials have said that under this Internet programme, an anomaly found in one aircraft of an airline may not be enough to warrant action by that airline but could warrant action if it turned up in other similar planes flown by other airlines.

"Almost all of what we know about aviation safety has been learned from after-the-fact investigations of accidents," Hinson said. "Yet, many times, there may have been advance warnings of unsafe conditions, which were unheeded because no one recognised their significance."

Asked if he thought a bomb or a mechanical failure caused the fatal crash of Trans World Airlines Flight 800 off Long Island last July 17, he said, "It would be very unwise for the administrator or anybody else for that matter to speculate out loud what may or may not have caused TWA 800."
He said the investigation was still going on and evidence being evaluated, adding, "Let it take you where it takes you."

He added that even if mechanical failure is found to be the cause, the planned new national anti-terrorist programme would still move ahead because of the growing need to improve the level of aviation security.
